scope_note: Every payload is parsed with json.loads() at generation time, and the broken one is asserted to fail parsing.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does the payload record about the second entry in the interfaces array?

options.text: It is enabled and carries a single address.
It is disabled but still carries a single address.
It is enabled and carries no addresses at all.
It is disabled and carries no addresses at all.

items.explanation: The second object in the array sets enabled to false and gives addresses an empty pair of brackets, so both readings point the same way: the interface is down and holds nothing. Option A describes the first entry instead, which is the ordinary wrong-element read when arrays are indexed by eye. Option B takes the correct enabled value but the wrong address list. Option C reverses both fields at once.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two of these readings of the JSON document are accurate? (Choose two.)

options.text: addresses on the first interface is an array holding one string.
location holds the JSON null value rather than an empty string.
management is an array of three settings rather than an object.
port holds the string "443" rather than a number.
interfaces holds a single object rather than a list of them.

items.explanation: Square brackets mark an array and the one element inside them is quoted, so addresses is an array of one string, and location reads null, which is JSON's own keyword for an absent value and is distinct from an empty pair of quotes. Option C misreads braces as brackets, since management groups named settings and is an object. Option D calls an unquoted 443 a string, when JSON numbers are never quoted. Option E ignores the brackets around the two interface objects.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why does the parser reject this document?

options.text: The vlans array may not hold bare numbers; each value needs quoting.
An object cannot be nested inside another object in JSON.
JSON booleans are written true and false, in lower case.
The last key in an object must be followed by a trailing comma.

items.explanation: JSON spells its booleans entirely in lower case, so True is not a keyword the parser recognises and the document fails at that line; the capitalised form comes from Python and is a frequent slip when a file is written by hand. Option A is wrong because unquoted numbers are exactly how JSON expresses them. Option B is contradicted by the uplink object, which nests legitimately. Option D inverts the rule, since a trailing comma is itself invalid.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. How many interface objects does this payload describe?
items.explanation: The interfaces array holds two brace-delimited objects, one per interface, each with its own name, enabled flag and address list. Option B counts only the first. Option C counts the key/value pairs inside one object rather than the objects themselves. Option D misreads the square brackets as braces, and the difference matters: an array can grow to hold more interfaces where a single object could not.
